metadata.title: When a Prediction Feeds Itself
metadata.description: Three simplified prediction loops shown one at a time: predictive policing, student risk prediction, and a traffic forecast for the road to Delphi. Each edge carries a link id (L1 to L10) and a polarity; each node's loop field says which loop it belongs to. Directions only, no sizes.
metadata.author: Mediterranean Travels

nodes.label: Predicted crime in a district
nodes.description: The model's forecast of how much crime will happen in a district.

nodes.label: Patrols sent to that district
nodes.description: How many officers and patrol hours the district gets.

nodes.label: Crimes recorded in that district
nodes.description: Crimes that were reported or discovered and written into police records. Records are not the same as crime.

nodes.label: True crime in the district
nodes.description: Outside factor, not part of the loop. Records rise with true crime and with patrols; the model cannot tell which.

nodes.label: Student's risk score
nodes.description: An early-warning model's estimate that the student will fail or drop out.

nodes.label: Placement in a lower-level course
nodes.description: How likely the student is to be placed in a less demanding course.

nodes.label: Access to challenging coursework
nodes.description: How much demanding material the student is taught.

nodes.label: Grades and test scores
nodes.description: The student's results, which feed the next risk score.

nodes.label: Predicted traffic at 9 AM on the Athens–Delphi road
nodes.description: The forecast published for 9 AM on the road to Delphi.

nodes.label: Drivers who leave earlier or take another road
nodes.description: Drivers who change their plans because of the forecast.

nodes.label: Traffic at 9 AM
nodes.description: How heavy the traffic actually is at 9 AM.

edges.description: Police send more patrols where the model predicts more crime.
More officers on the street discover and record more of the crime that is there.
The model is retrained on the records, so more records raise the next prediction.
Records rise with true crime and with patrols; the model cannot tell which.
A higher score makes a lower-level placement more likely.
The lower-level course offers less challenging work.
Students who are taught more challenging material tend to score higher on it.
Higher grades lower the risk score.
A forecast of heavy traffic sends more drivers out early or onto other roads.
The more drivers avoid 9 AM, the lighter the 9 AM traffic.
Next week's forecast is learned from this week's traffic.

loops.label: Loop 1
loops.description: No opposite links: a higher prediction brings more patrols, more records, and a still higher prediction, whatever the true crime rate.
loops.start_question: If the model predicts more crime here, what happens next?

loops.label: Loop 2
loops.description: Two opposite links cancel: a higher risk score leads, through less challenging work and lower grades, to a still higher risk score.
loops.start_question: If a student's risk score goes up, what happens next?

loops.label: Loop 3
loops.description: One opposite link: a forecast of heavy traffic leads to lighter traffic and a lower forecast next week, so the prediction defeats itself.
loops.start_question: If the forecast predicts heavy traffic at 9 AM, what happens next?

questions.question: Which change would weaken Loop 1?
choices: Send more patrols to every district
Train the model on crimes reported by victims and residents rather than on crimes discovered by patrols
Retrain the model every week instead of every month
questions.why: Records that do not depend on where the patrols went no longer carry L2's effect into L3; more patrols or more frequent retraining only feed the same loop.

questions.question: Which use of the risk score would turn Loop 2 from harm to help?
choices: Hide the score from the student
Keep the student in the challenging course and add tutoring when the score is high
questions.why: Adding support instead of lowering the placement replaces link L5's loss of challenging work with more help, so a high score leads to higher grades.

questions.question: Next Sunday the 9 AM forecast said "heavy traffic," and the road was light. What is the best explanation?
choices: Drivers acted on the forecast, so the jam it predicted did not form
questions.why: In a balancing loop a useful forecast can look wrong, because people change their behavior to avoid what it predicts.
